content: 1. Porter et al. (2015) reported no evidence of emergent resistance in HIV-1-infected adolescents treated with elvitegravir-based single-tablet regimens, as part of the GS-US-292-0106 trial (NCT01854775). 2. Gaur et al. (2016) evaluated the safety and efficacy of a single-tablet regimen containing elvitegravir, cobicistat, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide (E/C/F/TAF) in treatment-naïve HIV-1-infected adolescents through an open-label, single-arm trial (GS-US-292-1515, NCT02276612). 3. Batra et al. (2015) presented 24-week data from a Phase 3 clinical trial assessing E/C/F/TAF in HIV-positive adolescents, highlighting its safety and efficacy. 4. Kizito et al. (2015) and Shao et al. (2015) also contributed 24-week data from similar Phase 3 trials, further supporting the use of E/C/F/TAF in HIV-infected adolescents. 5. The IMPAACT P1083 study (2017) examined virological responses and resistance patterns over 12 months in HIV-infected children under two years receiving lopinavir/ritonavir-based antiretroviral therapy in Côte d'Ivoire and Burkina Faso. 6. Pressiat et al. (2017) identified suboptimal co-trimoxazole prophylactic concentrations in HIV-infected children, raising concerns about adherence to WHO guidelines. 7. Lombard et al. (2015) reported 48-week safety and efficacy data for a rilpivirine-based regimen in treatment-naïve HIV-infected adolescents as part of the PAINT Phase II trial. 8. Gopalan et al. (2017) highlighted the implications of sub-therapeutic nevirapine concentrations during antiretroviral treatment initiation in children, emphasizing the need for therapeutic drug monitoring. 9. Shiau et al. (2012) investigated maternal and infant antiretroviral regimens to prevent postnatal HIV-1 transmission, with 48-week follow-up data from the BAN randomized controlled trial. 10. The DART trial (2012) explored pregnancy and infant outcomes among HIV-infected women on long-term antiretroviral therapy (ART), with and without tenofovir. 11. The DOLPHIN-1 study (2018) compared dolutegravir versus efavirenz when initiating treatment in late pregnancy, providing interim analysis results. 12. IMPAACT 1026s (2018) and other studies assessed the pharmacokinetics, safety, and efficacy of antiretroviral regimens in pregnant women and their infants, focusing on outcomes such as HIV transmission and survival. 13. Ngoma et al. (2015) evaluated the efficacy of WHO recommendations for continued breastfeeding and maternal combination ART in preventing perinatal and postnatal HIV transmission in Zambia. 14. PROMISE 1077BF/1077FF trials (2015) examined the safety and efficacy of strategies to prevent perinatal HIV transmission, including maternal ART and infant prophylaxis. 15. Cohan et al. (2015) and Koss et al. (2015) studied the efficacy and safety of lopinavir/ritonavir versus efavirenz-based ART in HIV-infected pregnant Ugandan women, with additional analyses on preterm birth risk factors. 16. Samuel et al. (2014) investigated the impact of lopinavir/ritonavir-based ART versus efavirenz-based ART on malaria prevention in HIV-infected pregnant women. 17. Zash et al. (2018) compared the safety of dolutegravir and efavirenz initiated during pregnancy in Botswana, concluding that both regimens were similarly safe based on nationwide birth outcomes surveillance. 18. Thorne et al. 19. Dooley et al. (2015) examined the pharmacokinetics of efavirenz in pregnant women with and without tuberculosis co-infection, highlighting the complexities of co-treatment. 20. Bussmann et al. (2007) reported on pregnancy rates and birth outcomes among women on efavirenz-containing ART in Botswana. 21. Giuliano et al. (2017) identified high CMV IgG antibody levels as being associated with a lower CD4+ response to ART in HIV-infected women. 22. Andreotti et al. (2015) studied drug resistance mutations 18 months after discontinuation of nevirapine-based ART for preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission in Malawi. 23. Palombi et al. (2014) evaluated the impact of HBV or HCV co-infection in HIV-infected pregnant women receiving nevirapine-based ART in Malawi. 24. Various network diagrams summarized the trials informing outcomes such as viral suppression, CD4 cell count changes, mortality, AIDS-defining illnesses, and adverse events across different populations and treatment regimens. 25. The Cochrane Risk of Bias tool and other instruments were used to critically appraise the quality of randomized and non-randomized studies, ensuring robust evidence synthesis. This summary reflects the detailed findings and analyses from numerous clinical trials and studies, emphasizing their contributions to understanding HIV treatment and prevention in diverse populations.
